analysis.investment_thesis: Anup Engineering is a credible India capex-cycle beneficiary with 24.5% revenue CAGR and 22.4% net profit CAGR over five years, serving structurally growing end-markets (LNG, hydrogen, petrochemicals). However, sharply negative FY25 operating cash flow (−₹7 Cr) against ₹118 Cr reported profit and borrowings surging to ₹158 Cr signals working capital strain that must be resolved before this qualifies as a high-conviction compounder.
key_strengths: Revenue acceleration: FY25 revenue ₹733 Cr (+36% YoY), with 5Y CAGR of 24.5% clearing Fisher's 20%+ growth hurdle.
Technology differentiation: proprietary products (Helix changers, EMBaffle exchangers) in specialty process equipment suggest defensible niches beyond pure fabrication.
Debt discipline: D/E of 0.25 well within Fisher's 0.5 threshold; equity base growing steadily (₹323→₹636 Cr over 5 years).
key_risks: FY25 cash flow collapse: OCF −₹7 Cr and FCF −₹51 Cr despite ₹118 Cr net profit implies massive working capital build — execution risk on project-heavy revenue.
Borrowings jumped from ₹0 to ₹158 Cr and cash fell to ₹3 Cr; balance sheet headroom is thinning rapidly during the capex expansion phase.
ROE of 18.9% is slightly below Fisher's 20% threshold and net profit growth (22.4% CAGR) is slower than revenue growth, hinting at margin dilution as scale increases.
red_flags: FY25 operating cash flow turned sharply negative (−₹7 Cr) — a ₹176 Cr swing from FY24's ₹169 Cr OCF — despite strong reported earnings; classic project-based working capital trap.

Gross margin reported at just 3.79% vs operating margin of 17.9% implies extreme raw material pass-through, making margins sensitive to input cost volatility and customer concentration in project orders.
No disclosed R&D spending — Fisher demands innovation investment; 'technology products' branding is unvalidated without R&D line items.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Anup Engineering checks several Fisher boxes on the surface: double-digit revenue growth clearing 20%, an expanding operating income trend (₹70 Cr→₹168 Cr), low leverage, and exposure to secular Indian capex themes including hydrogen and LNG infrastructure. The company's specialty process equipment (heat exchangers, reactors, centrifuges) commands decent 17.9% operating margins, and the presence of proprietary technology products suggests more than a pure job-shop fabricator. Promoter holding at 40.9% with DII accumulation at 16.1% reflects reasonable institutional confidence.

The critical Fisher concern is cash flow quality. In FY25, the business generated ₹118 Cr of net profit but negative ₹7 Cr of operating cash — a ₹176 Cr OCF swing from FY24. This is typical of project-based industrial firms where revenue is recognized on completion but receivables and WIP balloon mid-cycle. Borrowings leapt to ₹158 Cr (from near-zero in FY22) while cash depleted to ₹3 Cr. Fisher insists on businesses that self-fund growth; Anup is currently funding growth via debt. At P/E 34.8x and EV/EBITDA 22.4x, the market is paying a premium for the growth story — justified only if cash conversion normalises in FY26. A HOLD is appropriate: the underlying franchise has genuine merit but requires proof that FY25 cash flow was a timing anomaly, not a structural deterioration.
